solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

parts.note: surface reading: a stroke or row drawn off to the edge of something
setter's reading: an actor's line spoken as an aside, meant to be heard by the audience but supposedly not by the others on stage

explanation.walkthrough: 'Line' sounds geometric, but it is a line of dialogue, and 'to one side' is an aside in the theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: An aside delivered by an actor so the audience hears it while other characters supposedly don't is exactly this theatrical device.

indicators.note: something that broke is smashed apart, so the name's letters are scattered and reassembled

parts.note: the Greek philosopher's name, used as letters

explanation.surface: A calculating machine has been smashed by the ancient philosopher Aristotle.
explanation.definitionFit: A totaliser is a machine that adds up figures, such as the betting tote, so it is a kind of calculator.

parts.note: a language spoken in Germany and Austria
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Someone notes which language is pertinent here: English.
explanation.definitionFit: Germane is a formal synonym meaning pertinent or bearing directly on the matter in hand.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to talk at length about nothing much
second meaning: a flat grid-patterned cake of fried potato

explanation.surface: Someone turns on the gas ring to cook a potato cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gas' looks like the cooker fuel, but in British slang to gas is to chatter idly.
explanation.definitionFit: To waffle is to ramble on emptily, and a potato waffle is a common British frozen fried snack.

clue.text: Loafer in crimson I raised, heel finally slipped into it

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising something lifts it so it reads from bottom to top, backwards
slipped into says one piece is slid inside the other

parts.note: crimson is a shade of red

indicators.note: finally points to the very last letter of the word heel

explanation.surface: A shoe called a loafer, in crimson, is lifted up and the heel slipped on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loafer' and 'heel' build a shoe picture, but the loafer here is a lazy person. RED and I are read upwards to give IDER, and L goes in to make IDLER.
explanation.definitionFit: A loafer is someone who idles about avoiding work, which is exactly what an idler does.

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifted means the word is turned to read from the bottom up

explanation.surface: The first prize has been lifted, as if stolen or held aloft.
explanation.definitionFit: A pot is slang for a trophy or cup, and also the pool of winnings, both kinds of reward.

clue.text: Body of work reporter and I reviewed, ending in article

indicators.note: something reviewed is gone over and reworked, so these letters are rearranged
ending in points to the last letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A journalist and I have reviewed a body of work, ending with a published article.
explanation.definitionFit: A repertoire is the full stock of pieces a performer or company is ready to perform, their collected output.

indicators.note: without ending says the word for beginning loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A celebrity's career starts but never seems to finish.
explanation.definitionFit: A star is a famous performer or public figure, a common synonym for someone celebrated.

parts.note: a tip is a piece of advice

explanation.surface: Someone sensed a piece of advice meant for an author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' looks like an author but is the pen itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A felt-tip is a pen with a fibre point, and a pen is something that writes.

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read literally: to munch on animal grease
second meaning: British slang for talk idly, from rhyming slang rabbit and pork for talk

explanation.surface: An odd instruction to eat some lard and a rabbit.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is the idiom read word for word. To rabbit, in Britain, is to chatter on.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to have a long casual gossip, while its words literally describe chomping on grease.

clue.text: Bag that's worn-out in large room

indicators.note: in places one word inside the other word

parts.note: a hall is a large room

explanation.surface: An old, shabby bag sits in a big room.
explanation.definitionFit: A holdall is a large soft travel bag that carries a bit of everything.

clue.text: Turner taking some Miro to Raphael

indicators.note: taking some means only a stretch of the following words is used

parts.note: the letters run across the end of Miro, all of to, and the start of Raphael

explanation.surface: The painter Turner borrows a picture by Miró to give to Raphael.
explanation.walkthrough: With Miró and Raphael alongside, 'Turner' reads as the English painter; here it is simply something that turns.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotor is the spinning part of a machine, such as a helicopter's blades, so it is a thing that turns.

clue.text: A setter is composing pieces of written work

indicators.note: composing means putting together in a new arrangement, so these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A crossword setter is writing some pieces of work.
explanation.definitionFit: Treatises are formal written works that examine a subject systematically, so they are pieces of written work.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a flat disc with a hole, fitted under a nut or bolt
second meaning: one who cleans clothes

explanation.surface: A laundry worker who belongs to a ring, a gang laundering money.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a small flat ring used in plumbing and machinery and a person or machine that cleans.

indicators.note: adjusted means altered and set differently, so these letters are moved around

explanation.surface: A car's gauge is reading deep, so it needs adjusting.
explanation.walkthrough: A motor is British slang for a car.
explanation.definitionFit: Speedo is the informal shortening of speedometer, the dashboard dial showing how fast a car travels.

indicators.note: messed means thrown into disorder, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Losing a final through one's own blunder is agonising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Messed up' looks like a single anagram signal, but only 'Messed' is; 'up' belongs to the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something agonising causes great distress or hurt, which is what painful describes.

clue.text: Tale is here in stale pudding

wordplay.note: in the word stale, the letters of tale come after the letter S

explanation.surface: A story turns up in a stale dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay describes where the word tale sits inside stale: after S. Afters is British slang for dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: Afters is the informal British term for the sweet course served at the end of a meal.

indicators.note: turned means twisted into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A bad skin rash has become hot and inflamed.
explanation.definitionFit: Harsh and severe both describe something stern, unpleasantly rough or demanding.

indicators.note: about means going around, so one word wraps the other

parts.note: hum is British slang for a bad smell

explanation.surface: A stink hangs around, and it's just right for rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Garbage' looks like rubbish that smells, but it means nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Hokum is nonsense or claptrap, and garbage is used figuratively for exactly that kind of worthless talk.

indicators.note: bags as a verb means puts into a bag, so one word holds the other

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Better bags are the right choice for rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bags' and 'waste' suggest bin liners, but 'bags' is a verb and 'waste' is to squander. R goes inside FITTER.
explanation.definitionFit: To fritter is to squander time or money on trifles, usually fritter away, which means to waste.

clue.text: Iron clothes clerk ordered for Mark

indicators.note: clothes as a verb means dresses, so one word wraps around the other

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

indicators.note: ordered means put into a new sequence, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone irons the clothes a clerk has ordered for a man called Mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iron clothes' reads as doing the ironing; 'Iron' is FE and 'clothes' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A freckle is a small brown spot on the skin, so it is a mark.

indicators.note: the word never hugs, or holds within it, the letters wanted

parts.note: found inside never, between its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A president's wife who refuses ever to give hugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First Lady' suggests a president's wife, but here it is the first woman in Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible, Eve was the first woman created, so she is literally the first lady.

clue.text: Nippy, while temperature beyond freezing, initially

indicators.note: beyond says the earlier pieces come after the later one, so they are placed behind it
initially points to the opening letter of the word freezing

parts.note: while and as both mean during the time that
T is the abbreviation for temperature

explanation.surface: It's nippy out, the temperature just above freezing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nippy' reads as chilly, matching the weather, but it means quick.
explanation.definitionFit: Nippy is informal British for quick and agile, as in a nippy little car, so it means fast.

clue.text: Flying KLM's safer tho' it maintains a constant temperature

indicators.note: flying suggests things tossed through the air, so the letters land in a new order

parts.note: the airline's name, safer and the clipped tho, used as letters

explanation.surface: Flying with the Dutch airline KLM is safer, though cabin temperature stays steady.
explanation.walkthrough: KLM is the Dutch national airline.
explanation.definitionFit: A vacuum bottle keeps drinks hot or cold for hours, holding its contents at a steady warmth or chill.
